t65w_lm1p1e: If you weren't loved well as a child, "love your inner child" might sound like nonsense. You can sincerely want the best for your little one, hug them in your imagination, or miss them, and still feel none of the warmth people mean when they say love. That doesn't close the door. It means starting with smaller things.
t65w_lm1p1f: Here's a hard one. If nobody really loved you growing up, then "love your inner child" can land like a joke you're not in on. You might want good things for your little one, picture hugging them, miss them, and still not feel anything warm at all. So start smaller than love.
t65w_lm1p1g: Love your inner child, they say. And if you weren't loved much as a child yourself, that can sound like nonsense, because where would the love come from? You might care what happens to your little one, picture holding them, miss them, and feel none of the warm glow people describe. That's a real starting point, and it calls for smaller steps.
t65w_lm1p2e: If picturing a caring grown-up makes things worse, more scary or more lonely, don't force it. Go for the least cruel thing a decent adult could do instead, and do that. Nobody's grading you on whether you were loved enough as a child. Think of it as scaffolding, something to lean on while there's room for warmth to show up, with no promise about when.
t65w_lm1p3d: Taking the hostility out leaves room for warmth. And what people most often say helped them is letting their defenses down, when they're ready, after the guarding part has been heard. If love has never felt safe, the ego can work like a bouncer whose whole job is keeping that feeling out, and vulnerability is the gap it needs. Sometimes the warmth isn't gone at all. It's behind a cold part that's guarding something, and once you hear what that is, it may step aside.
t65w_lm1p3e: Once the hostility is gone, there's space for warmth. People say the biggest help is lowering their defenses, by choice, after the guarding part has had its say (see Hear the Protective Part First). For someone who's never felt safe being loved, the ego can act like a rigid security guard for the feeling itself, and vulnerability is the opening it needs. The warmth might just be eclipsed, by a cold part that's protecting something. Two other approaches come up a lot in spiritual and trauma-recovery circles.
t65w_lm2p1d: Some people don't just say love feels out of reach. They say, "No. I hate myself." I'm not going to argue you out of that. If hatred is what you find in there, it deserves an honest hearing. But I don't want to skip something else. If you chose to open this article, come to therapy, ask somebody for help, or try again after deciding you were hopeless, something in you wanted something to be different.
t65w_lm3p1d: Rumi says you have to keep breaking your heart until it stays open. Some people find that deep grieving gives way to warmth or connection, or to a feeling in the body of being held by the universe. That's a description of an experience, though, not proof of how the body produces it. And love can open grief from the other side: being cared for may bring sadness for the care that was missing, which doesn't mean the love failed. Stay with it while you're present and still have a choice, and slow down if it starts to swamp you.
t65w_lm3p1e: There's a Rumi line about breaking your heart until it stays open. For some people that's close to literal: they grieve hard, and what's underneath turns out to be warmth, or a bodily sense of being held by the universe. The feeling is real, even though it can't tell you what's happening physically. It can go the other way too, when someone's kindness brings up grief for the kindness you never got. That's not the love failing. Go only as far as you can while you're still present and choosing, and slow down when it starts to drown you.
t65w_lm4p3c: If you're curious, follow the curiosity rather than pretending to believe. Read people from different traditions. Meet people whose lives make you wonder what they found. Pay attention to the fruits: does their path seem to make them more loving, honest and grounded, braver about suffering, or mostly more certain they've got the right explanation?
t65w_lm4p3d: Not everybody needs to go looking for something deeper. But if you're curious, I'd say follow that instead of trying to believe something. Read people from a few different traditions. Spend time with people whose lives make you wonder what they found, and watch what their path does to them. Do they get more loving and honest, steadier and braver around suffering? Or mostly more sure they're right?
t65w_lm4p4c: Sometimes the problem isn't that care is absent. The whole available horizon of life feels too small, and a meal or a boundary or one kind sentence can help without answering the question underneath: "Why should I want this life at all?" Take that question seriously. What would have to be possible for being alive to feel worth discovering, not just enduring?
t65w_lm4p5c: Curiosity can be enough here, something like "Other people say they've felt a depth of love or peace that I never have. I don't know if I believe their explanation. But what if the experience is possible for me?" Don't assume the limits of what you've felt so far are the limits of what's possible.
t65w_fg1p1a: For a lot of people, healing eventually includes some kind of forgiveness, or at least getting out from under active resentment. It can't be put on a schedule, though, and you don't need it first to be safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable or get better. Resentment can narrow what you see and keep your little one organized around the injury. But forcing yourself to forgive early tends to turn into an enlightened performance while the wound goes underground.
t65w_fg1p1b: For a lot of people, healing includes some kind of forgiveness eventually, or at least getting out from under the resentment. It doesn't run on a schedule, though, and you don't need it before you can be safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable or recover. Resentment can shrink what you're able to see and keep your little one organized around the injury. Then again, pushing yourself to forgive early tends to become an enlightened performance, with the wound gone underground.
t65w_fg1p2a2: It can help to see how someone's conditioning, history, pain and capacity shaped the harmful thing they did. Given everything they'd become by that moment, it was the only move they had available. Hurt people often pass on pain they never processed. When you can see that for yourself, instead of being told to, forgiveness sometimes shows up on its own, and the rage that held them as uniquely to blame can soften into something more accurate.
t65w_fg1p2b: What tends to help is seeing how a person's conditioning, history, pain and capacity shaped the harm they did. By that moment, given everything they'd become, it was the only move their nature had on offer. Hurt people often pass on pain they never dealt with. And once that's something you can see, not a rule somebody handed you, forgiveness may come on its own, while the rage that made them uniquely guilty softens into something truer.
t65w_fg1p3a: That doesn't make what they did harmless, and it doesn't mean no other option existed in theory. It means punishing them can't go back and create the awareness or support they didn't have. The useful work is repairing what can be repaired, and making a different response more available now. Accountability stays, and the harm is real.
t65w_fg1p3b: Boundaries, legal consequences, moral judgment, distance and permanent no-contact can all still be right. You can understand how they got that way, hold them responsible, never speak to them again, and forgive them. "I get how you became this" can sit right next to "and now I get why I can't rely on you for this."
t65w_fg1p4a3: Forgiving yourself works the same way, and when it's hard, forgiving other people tends to be harder too. Own what you did and its impact, without taking on what wasn't yours. Let the remorse register and repair what you can. After that you're allowed to stop punishing yourself, and the responsibility stays yours. Some harms take years. Living permanently inside resentment is its own trap, so come back to the question of how they became capable of it now and then, until the understanding is real enough to change how you feel.
t65w_le1p1a3: Your little one often gets loudest in the gap after one life has ended and before the next one has formed. Think of a breakup, a move to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, a child leaving home. Leaving a family or a community can do it too, and so can staying in one on new terms. Tibetan Buddhism calls an in-between state a bardo. You don't have to buy its teachings about death and rebirth to use the everyday part: endings leave a stretch with no familiar identity and nothing clear to replace it yet.
t65w_le1p2a2: So ask yourself what has really ended, and what you're still trying to keep going. What isn't known yet? What is your little one afraid will happen in the gap? And what small ritual or practical act could mark the ending without pretending you know what comes next? Don't force a new identity just because not knowing feels unbearable. You can keep your routines, take care of your body, grieve what ended and stay with your little one while the next life takes shape.
t65w_le1p3b: Missing someone doesn't have to become another problem to solve, either. Sometimes the ache itself can turn into a cue for love. If love is there, let "I miss you" become "I love you," or try a simple wish: "May you be safe. May you be held in love." You can picture them, or just feel the direction of the care.
t65w_le1p4c: This is about what happens in you. It doesn't depend on them receiving anything, and it doesn't replace grieving or contact; you still keep your boundaries and do the practical things. If sending love starts making you compulsive, or a little unreal, make it simpler: "I miss you, and I care." And you can turn some of that same care toward the part of you that's still here.
t65w_ba1p1a: Reparenting usually gets framed as something you do alone or with a therapist. But your little one got hurt in relationships, and a relational injury can only heal so far in isolation. Sometimes one person ends up carrying a lot of the borrowed-adult jobs at once: food, planning, health decisions, rides, social life, reassurance, protection, company, or just the sense that somebody competent is next to you. Having someone like that when you're struggling can be a huge blessing.
t65w_ba1p2a2: Over time, reparenting can help you take in some of what that person has been modeling for you, and practice it yourself. Other jobs can be shared around, with friends, community, professionals or services, routines and plain old tools. Which of those jobs can become more yours? Which are healthiest shared? Which belong inside the relationship? The point is for your little one to feel reliable care through more than one door, while the relationship itself stays as precious as it is.

## How Much Happiness Do You Know Is Possible?

Part of love is wanting someone to be well, and how far that wish can reach depends partly on what kind of happiness you know is possible. If the happiness you know is food, safety, affection, friends, work that means something and some help when you need it, then wanting those things for somebody is love. Babies get some of this already. Practical love matters a lot.

But a big spiritual experience can show you a kind of peace, or a love, you didn't know existed, and then "I want you to be happy" suddenly means something much bigger. That's partly why loving-kindness meditation can sound almost comically simple to someone who's never been near what it's pointing at, and so powerful to someone who has. Saying "may you be happy" over and over isn't automatically some profound love. It's one way of finding that deeper love and growing it.

# How to Forgive Without Forgetting

For a lot of people, healing eventually includes some kind of forgiveness, or at least getting out from under active resentment. Resentment can narrow what you see and keep your little one organized around the injury. But forcing yourself to forgive early tends to turn into an enlightened performance while the wound goes underground.
